text: Metformin is the first-line medication for type 2 diabetes. It reduces hepatic glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity. Typical starting dose is 500mg once daily, titrating to 2000mg daily.
Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. They are second-line when metformin alone is insufficient. Risk of hypoglycemia is higher compared to metformin.
Insulin therapy is indicated when oral medications fail to achieve glycemic control. Basal insulin (e.g., glargine) is typically started at 10 units or 0.1-0.2 units/kg daily.
Fasting plasma glucose target: 80-130 mg/dL. Postprandial glucose target: <180 mg/dL. HbA1c target: <7.0% for most adults with type 2 diabetes.
Hypoglycemia is defined as glucose <70 mg/dL. Symptoms include sweating, palpitations, confusion, and hunger. Severe hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) requires immediate medical attention.
Ethiopian staple diet includes injera made from teff. Teff has a lower glycemic index than wheat or maize. Pairing injera with shiro, gomen, or lean meat helps reduce post-meal glucose spikes.
The Ethiopian Ministry of Health recommends: reduce sugar-sweetened beverages, choose whole grains, eat at least 5 portions of fruits and vegetables daily, and limit salt intake.
A diabetes-friendly plate should be: 50% non-starchy vegetables, 25% lean protein, and 25% complex carbohydrates. This helps maintain stable blood glucose levels throughout the day.
Adults with type 2 diabetes should engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, spread over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 consecutive days without activity.
Resistance training twice a week improves insulin sensitivity and glycemic control. Exercises like bodyweight squats, wall push-ups, and resistance band work are effective.
Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness. Annual eye examinations are essential for all patients with type 2 diabetes.
Diabetic foot complications can be prevented through daily foot checks, proper footwear, and annual podiatry assessment. Any foot ulcer requires immediate medical evaluation.
Medication adherence is the single most important self-care behavior in diabetes management. Consistent adherence reduces HbA1c by an average of 0.5-1.0% compared to inconsistent use.
Patients who maintain a 7-day medication streak are 3 times more likely to reach their target HbA1c within 3 months. Each dose taken on time builds sustainable glucose control.
Self-monitoring of blood glucose is recommended for all patients on insulin or sulfonylureas. For others, structured monitoring helps identify glucose patterns and guides treatment adjustments.
Consistent glucose tracking helps identify patterns. High fasting readings may indicate insufficient basal insulin or dawn phenomenon. High post-meal readings suggest meal composition adjustments.
Ethiopian traditional medicine should be disclosed to healthcare providers. Some herbal remedies can interact with diabetes medications and affect blood glucose levels.
Stress management is important for glycemic control. Cortisol and other stress hormones can raise blood glucose. Regular prayer, meditation, or community gatherings can help manage stress.
Adequate sleep (7-8 hours per night) is associated with better glycemic control. Poor sleep increases insulin resistance and appetite-regulating hormone disruption.

Diabetes self-management education is a right of every person with diabetes. Understanding the condition leads to better outcomes. Patients should know their target glucose ranges and what to do when levels are out of range.
